provoke

pra-VOHK / rhymes with soak · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To provoke someone or something is to deliberately act in a way that triggers a strong reaction, especially anger or irritation.

The comedian's opening joke provoked a storm of laughter.

Worked Example

When the visiting team's fans sat in the home crowd's section and began chanting loudly, their presence provoked an angry storm of yelling and shoving from the home supporters.

Provoke fits perfectly because it emphasizes the deliberate action (sitting in the wrong section, chanting) designed to trigger a strong emotional reaction (anger and aggression). Simpler words like irritate would miss both the intentionality and the intensity.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

trigger: To trigger something is to set off a sudden strong reaction the way one domino tips the rest - and a trigger can be entirely accidental. Provoke adds intent: to provoke is to deliberately poke at someone until the strong reaction comes. An earthquake triggers panic; a taunt provokes it.

irritate: To irritate someone is to annoy them steadily - a dripping tap, a tapping pencil - wearing patience down bit by bit without ever exploding. Provoke is sharper and deliberate: to provoke is to act on purpose to set off one strong, immediate reaction. Irritation builds slowly; provocation aims for the burst.

antagonize: To antagonize someone is to deliberately turn them into a lasting enemy - the word is about the hostility you build toward yourself. Provoke aims at a reaction, not a relationship: you provoke an outburst in a moment, while antagonizing someone makes them your ongoing opponent.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

soothe: to calm someone's anger or distress

pacify: to make an angry person calm and peaceful

Where it sits · how angry the target becomes — annoy → provoke → infuriate → enrage

annoy vs. provoke: Annoy is much weaker than provoke: annoying someone merely bothers them, while provoking them deliberately triggers a strong, heated reaction.

infuriate vs. provoke: Infuriate is stronger than provoke — to provoke someone sparks their anger, but to infuriate them drives that anger into open fury.

enrage vs. provoke: Enrage sits at the top, well above provoke: a provoked person bristles and snaps back, while an enraged person has been pushed into blind, uncontrollable rage.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — pro-

Prefix — pro-: forth, forward (Latin)

Root — voke

Root — voke: to call (from Latin vocāre, 'to call'; the same root is spelled voc- in vocal and vocabulary)

Put it together

Put it together: Pro- ('forth') + voke ('to call,' from Latin vocāre — the same root spelled voc- in vocal and vocabulary): provoke literally means 'to call forth' — to deliberately call a strong reaction, usually anger or irritation, out of someone.

Use the root in a new word: vocal

Use the root in a new word: vocal: A vocal fan calls out opinions loudly — the same Latin root vocāre, 'to call,' lives inside provoke, which literally means to call forth a reaction.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral / everyday

Use provoke when someone deliberately stirs up a strong emotional reaction, especially anger. For mild annoyance or accidental upsets, simpler words like irritate or annoy are more precise. For deliberate hostility-building, antagonize might fit better.
